newsitem.title: USA: Records smashed in U.S. balloonist's attempt.
newsitem.headline: Records smashed in U.S. balloonist's attempt.

text.p: Steve Fossett's aborted attempt to circle the earth in a balloon that ended in a bumpy landing in India on Monday set records for distance and duration and provided lessons for the adventurer's next try, his team said.
A larger balloon may be needed to fly higher and faster than Fossett's "Solo Spirit" could and the balloonist may have to carry more propane to keep aloft longer.
"A larger envelope (balloon) will allow him to go even higher," British balloon designer Alan Noble said.

Fossett's "low-tech" $300,000 balloon had a supposed altitude ceiling of 18,000 feet (5,500 metres) but he pushed it to a height of 24,000 feet (7,300 metres) and reached speeds in excess of 100 mph (160 kph).
With a higher ceiling he could catch even faster winds in the jetstream. But flying higher could be even less comfortable inside the type of cramped, unpressurized gondola flown by Fossett.

"We knew the heaters wouldn't work" at high altitude, exhausted headquarters manager Bo Kemper said. Kemper, who spoke to Fossett from the lone telephone in a village in India near where he landed, said Fossett endured sub-zero F (under -18 C) temperatures at times.
Fossett said he planned on spending the night in the local police chief's guest house.

Noble, the designer with British-based Cameron Balloons, said he wanted to know why Fossett had to burn fuel at times during the daytime when solar heat normally would be adequate to maintain altitude.

Kemper said the 52-year-old former Chicago commodities broker had little idea that his voyage captured newspaper headlines and was followed by tens of thousands of people on the Internet. Kemper said the Smithsonian's Air and Space Museum wanted to put the "Solo Spirit" on display.

Pinned to the walls of the Chicago headquarters at Loyola University were maps tracing Fossett's 10,000-mile (16,000 km) voyage over 15 countries and the Atlantic Ocean over six days, two hours and 49 minutes.

Fossett, who began his journey last Monday night in St. Louis, Missouri, broke his own world record for distance traveled in a balloon and outlasted the previous record for continuous manned balloon flight -- six days and 16 minutes -- set in 1981 by Americans Ben Abruzzo and Troy Bradley.

Fossett had to detour around most of Libya when its government dragged its feet on granting permission for an overflight, causing him to use more fuel and to take a more southerly route that carried him into India and towards the dangerous Himalayan Mountain range.

Rather than risk skirting the Himalayas or landing in China, which also had not granted overflight permission, he chose to land in India. Before landing, he had to survive thunderstorms that could have turned the balloon into "confetti," Kemper said.

Richard Branson, the British tycoon whose circumnavigation attempt in a high-tech balloon with a pressurized capsule ended shortly after it began in Morocco on Jan. 8, relayed a message to Fossett that the attempt had been "brilliant."
Branson has said he would try again and an Australian effort was also under way.
